references.note: States the conjecture that finitely many linear forms a_i + b_i·n with no congruence obstruction are simultaneously prime infinitely often. The pairs (q, 2q−1) and (q, 4q−1) are two-form instances; the conjecture is unproved. The link is the encyclopedia entry that gives the citation; the paper itself was not read.
references.title: L. E. Dickson, A new extension of Dirichlet's theorem on prime numbers, Messenger of Mathematics 33, pp. 155–161 (dated 1903 or 1904 depending on the source)

references.note: The conjectural asymptotic count of n ≤ x at which several polynomials are simultaneously prime. A count of that shape, with an error term small enough to localise to (n, 2n−10], is what would give the every-interval form; it is a heuristic, not a theorem.
references.title: P. T. Bateman and R. A. Horn, A heuristic asymptotic formula concerning the distribution of prime numbers, Math. Comp. 16 (1962), 363–367

references.note: Definition: a Cunningham chain of the second kind is a sequence of primes with p_{i+1} = 2p_i − 1, so (q, 2q−1) is one of length two. The entry derives the infinitude of chains of each length only from Dickson's conjecture or Schinzel's hypothesis H.
references.title: Cunningham chain (Wikipedia)

references.note: The sequence of the q in the first alternative (2, 3, 7, 19, 31, 37, 79, 97, …). The entry records no proof that it is infinite.
references.title: OEIS A005382: Primes p such that 2p−1 is also prime

literature_proposed.summary: Open. The statement asks, in every interval (n, 2n−10] with n ≥ 1092, for a prime q with 2q−1 prime (m = 2q−2) or with 4q−1 prime (m = 4q−2). Each alternative is a pair of linear forms covered by Dickson's conjecture, and the Bateman–Horn heuristic predicts about C·n/(log n)^2 such q per interval, but no proof is known even that infinitely many primes q have 2q−1 or 4q−1 prime (the same status as Sophie Germain primes and twin primes); sieve methods for two simultaneous primes of this kind are obstructed by the parity problem. So no proof of this statement, which is stronger than infinitude, is in the literature. I did not find this exact every-interval statement listed anywhere as a named problem. Checked by exact computation for every n from 1092 to 10^7 (no failure; at least 20 admissible m in every interval).

statement.text:
import Mathlib
import Nodes.«spec-001a7622».Context

/-- A necessary condition for the calm-point hole `variant-cce9b284--h6` of the repair-walk route
to Erdős 257 (its "Set 9"), stated on its own because it is an open prime-pair conjecture.
Every interval `(n, 2n - 10]` with `n ≥ 1092` contains an `m = 2q - 2` or an `m = 4q - 2` with
`q` and `m + 1` both prime: a prime `q` with `2q - 1` prime and `n < 2q - 2 ≤ 2n - 10`, or with
`4q - 1` prime and `n < 4q - 2 ≤ 2n - 10`. By the structure lemma for calm points (annex
`e0c02cd3…` on the hole: a calm `m ≥ 1092` has `m + 1` prime and `(m + 2)/2` or `(m + 2)/4`
prime) the hole implies this statement. This statement does not imply the hole: a calm point
needs further conditions at `m + 3, m + 4, …`. It is a two-form instance of Dickson's conjecture
(the pair `q, 2q - 1` is a Cunningham chain of the second kind of length two) in a quantitative,
every-dyadic-interval form; even the infinitude of such `q` is not known. Since `q` is prime,
`q ≥ 2`, so the natural-number subtractions `2*q - 2`, `2*q - 1`, `4*q - 2`, `4*q - 1` are exact. -/
theorem dyadic_prime_pairs :
  ∀ n : ℕ, 1092 ≤ n → ∃ q : ℕ, q.Prime ∧
     ((n < 2*q - 2 ∧ 2*q + 8 ≤ 2*n ∧ (2*q - 1).Prime) ∨
      (n < 4*q - 2 ∧ 4*q + 8 ≤ 2*n ∧ (4*q - 1).Prime)) := by
  sorry
